# Performance: 1,000,000 points, before and after

**What is measured, how, and why some numbers are not what they seem:** `docs/experiments.md`
(checked before measuring) and `docs/decisions.md` P1–P4. Script: `perf/run-perf.ts`
(`pnpm perf:before`, `pnpm perf:after`); raw results: `perf/results-*.json`; console output:
`perf/output-*.txt`. The table below is generated from the result files by `pnpm perf:report`.

¹ DevTools CPU throttling does not apply to Web Workers, and Chrome refuses to throttle a worker
target (`docs/experiments.md` §2). The measured first render of the worker version is therefore
optimistic. The adjusted row adds `(4 − 1) × worker busy time` — what it would be if the worker ran
×4 slower too. It is an upper bound (it assumes all worker time is on the critical path).
² What Chrome Task Manager shows as the tab's memory = macOS `footprint` of the tab's renderer
process (the dedicated worker runs in the same process). The tab's process is the renderer with the
most CPU time. **Correction:** the first measurements summed all three renderer processes of the
headless browser (the tab plus two others of ~11 and ~24 MB) and called that "tab memory"; the
author's manual Task Manager screenshot showed much less and exposed it. After v1 was measured only
with the old method, hence "n/a". Manual Task Manager screenshots: `perf/screenshots/`.
³ Shown only to make the trap visible: CDP `JSHeapUsedSize` counts neither typed-array backing
stores nor the worker's heap (`docs/experiments.md` §4), so it reports a fake −97%.

## Manual cross-check: Chrome Task Manager (taken by the author)

The author's everyday Google Chrome (not headless, no CPU throttling, Retina display), a fresh
incognito window per page so each page gets its own renderer process (different process IDs), the
1M-point run fully drawn, ~10 s idle. Values transcribed from the screenshots:

| Page | Task Manager "Memory" | "JavaScript memory" | Process ID | Screenshot |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `/runs/long-1m?impl=naive` | 131 MB | 101,936 KB | 65886 | `perf/screenshots/task-manager-naive.png` |
| `/runs/long-1m` | 72.4 MB | 4,096 KB | 67245 | `perf/screenshots/task-manager-after.png` |

Agrees with the automated tab footprint (136 → 75 MB). Two notes:
- Task Manager's "JavaScript memory" column shows only the page's main-thread heap: the worker's
  ~31 MB of columns are not in the 4 MB — the same trap as `JSHeapUsedSize` (`docs/experiments.md`
  §4). The "Memory" column does include the worker.
- A first pair of screenshots was discarded: the second page had been loaded into the **same**
  renderer process as the first (same process ID), so it carried the first page's heap (180 MB
  for the optimized page). Closing the tab was not enough; closing the incognito window was.
  Those screenshots were also not committed because they showed unrelated personal tabs.

## What changed between "before" and "after", and what it did

| Change | Effect in the numbers |
|---|---|
| Generation, normalization, EMA and downsampling moved to a **Web Worker** | Total Blocking Time ≈ 1.5 s → ≈ 35 ms: the page stays responsive while 1M points load. The work itself did not get faster (see the adjusted first render: −6%), it just stopped blocking the main thread. |
| **Columnar Float64Array** instead of 1M `{step, loss, lr, grad_norm}` objects; typed arrays **transferred**, not copied | Tab memory 136 → 75 MB. The worker holds the normalized columns (~31 MB per `measureUserAgentSpecificMemory`); the main thread holds only a few thousand points per chart. |
| **Own M4 downsampling** to ≤ 4 points per device-pixel column instead of handing 1M points to uPlot | uPlot already collapses points per pixel internally (`docs/experiments.md` §1), so drawing was never the bottleneck: zoom and hover stay where they were. The gain is that the main thread never has to hold or traverse 1M points. |
| Readout in its own component (after v1 → final) | after v1 had a **hover regression** (6.6 ms vs ≈ 3.5 ms naive): every pointer move re-rendered all three charts because the readout lived in the chart's state. Moving it into a small component brought hover back to the naive level. |

## Traces

Open in Chrome DevTools → Performance → *Load profile*: `perf/trace-before.json`,
`perf/trace-after.json` (and `perf/trace-after-v1.json`). Each is one extra run of the same
scenario (load → 20 hover moves → drag-zoom) with CPU ×4; tracing adds overhead, so the table
uses the 5 untraced runs. Cross-check from the traces (`EventDispatch` durations of `mousemove`,
`mouseup`) is stored in each result file under `traceEventDispatchMs`.

### What the traces show (author's DevTools screenshot: `perf/screenshots/devtools-traces-before-after.png`)

The screenshot shows the traces recorded at commit 48db2c2. The files in `perf/` were re-recorded
with the final measurement (same scenario), so their exact numbers differ slightly from the screenshot.

Left `trace-before.json`, right `trace-after.json`, values as shown by the DevTools Summary for the
whole recording:

| | before (naive) | after |
|---|---|---|
| Scripting | 2,014 ms | 414 ms |
| Main thread time (localhost + unattributed) | 1,888.4 + 430.7 ms | 320.4 + 522.3 ms |
| LCP / INP / CLS (DevTools Insights) | 0.20 s / 42 ms / 0 | 0.22 s / 28 ms / 0 |

- Naive: one ~1.5 s long task at the start (generation on the main thread), then conversion and
  drawing. After: the same work sits in the `dataWorker-….js` track; the main thread has only short
  tasks. The long "frame" right after navigation in the after trace is a period with nothing new to
  paint (skeleton shown) while the worker computes — the main thread is free (TBT ≈ 35 ms).
- **LCP is the wrong metric here**: it is ~0.2 s in both versions because the LCP element is text,
  not the chart canvas. By Core Web Vitals both pages are "fast", while the naive one shows the
  chart only after ~1.7 s. Hence the custom `chart:first-draw` mark.
- INP comes from the drag-zoom (mousedown/mouseup); hover is not part of INP (`docs/experiments.md` §3).
- Absolute times in the traces are higher than in the table: tracing (CPU sampling, also in the
  worker) adds overhead, which is why the table uses the five untraced runs.

## History and honesty notes

- The first baseline (`perf/results-before-v1-superseded.json`, tag `perf-baseline`) was measured
  with the first version of the generator. In stage 4 the generator was rewritten to be bit-exact
  across JS engines (Math.exp/log/cos differ between Node and Chrome), which changed the data and
  made generation slower (Irwin–Hall noise: 12 random numbers per sample). Both "before" and
  "after" were therefore re-measured on the **same commit**, the naive pipeline being kept at
  `?impl=naive` for exactly this reason. The old file is kept, not deleted.
- The final table was re-measured on the final code, after stage 5 had added UI (freshness clock,
  "Go to step", smoothing check); the previous run (commit 48db2c2) is in git history and within noise
  of it.
- The mock "server" (generation) runs in the client here; in a real deployment it would be a
  network response, and parsing/transfer would replace generation in the first-render cost.
- Headless Chrome does not wait for a 60 Hz vsync, so hover/zoom "to next paint" times do not
  include the up-to-16 ms a real display adds.
